strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful structural setting, M-convex action sets, where the open problem of finite polynomial-in-d regret can be partially resolved. The O(d log d) bound is significant relative to prior O(d log T) and exp(O(d log d)) guarantees.
The technical idea is elegant: M-convex exchange properties convert optimality feedback into pairwise ordering constraints, and the volume/order-simplex argument yields a clean finite mistake bound.
The corruption extension is conceptually appealing. Detecting inconsistent feedback via cycles in the induced directed graph gives an adaptive O((C+1)d log d) guarantee without knowing C.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with useful warm-up analysis, clear relation to prior work, and an honest discussion of remaining gaps such as the log d factor and stronger corruption models.
weaknesses: The algorithmic status of the O(d log d) method is not fully rigorous. The paper relies on the exact center of gravity, then notes it is #P-hard and gestures to approximate randomized methods, but does not formally state or prove the regret guarantee for the implementable approximate version.

The tie-breaking/perturbation argument around the center of gravity is under-specified. Since the volume-shrinkage proof depends on cutting through the true centroid, an arbitrary small perturbation with distinct coordinates needs a more careful quantitative treatment.

The corruption model uses regret against the actually observed action, which can be suboptimal under corruptions and may make the bound less directly comparable to standard regret to the uncorrupted optimum. The manuscript notes equivalence up to C, but the presentation should more carefully handle signs and constants.

The lower bound adaptation to the M-convex case is brief and relies on embedding an M-natural-convex instance into one higher dimension without giving enough detail to verify preservation of regret and the feasible-set construction.

The contribution is theoretically useful but somewhat specialized: the result depends heavily on M-convex structure and does not address general polyhedral/combinatorial action sets or the cumulative-suboptimality corruption model considered in prior work.

strengths: The main uncorrupted argument is elegant and plausible: M-convex local exchange optimality converts each observation into pairwise ordering constraints, and the center-of-gravity/volume argument gives a clean O(d log d) mistake bound once the assumptions hold.

The paper identifies a meaningful structural regime for online inverse linear optimization. Matroids and bounded integer allocation sets are natural examples, so the restriction to M-convex action sets is not vacuous.
The corruption extension has a simple and intuitive mechanism: cycles in the learned ordering graph certify inconsistency, enabling restarts without knowing C.
The writing is generally clear, with the algorithms, regret metric, and relationship to prior O(d log T) and exponential finite bounds explained well.
weaknesses: The distinct-components assumption is treated as a minor technicality, but it appears material. With ties, the ordering graph can contain cycles even under uncorrupted optimal feedback, and the proposed perturbation argument is not enough for a horizon-independent finite regret guarantee because cumulative regret can scale with T unless the perturbation is controlled relative to all future feasible sets.

The claimed polynomial-time implementability of the O(d log d) algorithm is underdeveloped. Exact center-of-gravity computation is acknowledged as #P-hard, but the paper only gestures to approximate randomized methods and does not give a formal approximate-center version of Lemma 4.1/Theorem 4.2 with constants, failure probability, or oracle assumptions.

The oracle/computational model is imprecise. The text claims optimization and update steps over M-convex sets can be done in polynomial time from membership access, but this is not justified carefully and may depend on additional boundedness or representation assumptions.

The corruption model and regret definition are somewhat unsatisfactory. Regret is defined using the possibly corrupted action xt, so corrupted rounds can contribute negative regret; the discussion that this is essentially equivalent to regret against the uncorrupted optimum is informal and hides additive/sign issues that should be made precise.

The lower bound is only sketched by reduction through M-natural-convex embedding. The proof does not spell out how the objective, actions, and regret transfer under the added dimension, which is important because the paper uses the lower bound to claim near-tightness.

The significance is moderate rather than broad: the result is specialized to M-convex action sets, no empirical or applied demonstration is provided, and the most practically relevant robust setting with cumulative suboptimality is left open.

Limitations are mentioned mainly as future work, but key limitations such as exact center-of-gravity infeasibility, reliance on distinct objective coordinates, and representation/oracle requirements should be treated more explicitly. No material ethics concerns are apparent.

strengths: The paper makes a clear and meaningful theoretical contribution: it gives a finite O(d log d) regret bound for online inverse linear optimization under M-convex action sets, improving over prior finite bounds with exponential dimension dependence in this structured setting.

The main technical idea is elegant and well motivated. The paper combines the local exchange characterization of optimality for M-convex sets with a center-of-gravity volume-shrink argument, yielding a concise explanation for why only O(d log d) informative mistakes are possible.

The corruption-robust extension is a valuable addition. Detecting inconsistency through cycles in the induced directed graph is natural, does not require knowing C in advance, and gives a clean O((C+1)d log d) guarantee.

The paper situates the contribution well relative to online inverse optimization, contextual recommendation/search, and discrete convex analysis. The examples involving matroids and bounded integer allocations help justify the relevance of M-convex action sets.

The presentation is generally strong for a theory paper: the algorithms are simple, the proof structure is easy to follow, and the figures help explain the order-simplex and corruption-detection arguments.
The paper includes a matching lower bound up to a log d factor for the M-convex case, which makes the theoretical picture more complete.
weaknesses: The main O(d log d) algorithm relies on computing the center of gravity of a polytope, which the paper acknowledges is #P-hard exactly. The discussion of randomized approximate centroid computation is brief, and the formal regret guarantee is not fully restated for the implementable approximate version.

The corruption setting uses regret against the actually observed action x_t, which can be less standard and potentially less meaningful when x_t is corrupted. The paper argues equivalence up to O(C), but the central theorem would be clearer if stated directly for the optimal-action regret R*_T as well.

The lower bound section is quite terse and mostly appeals to adaptation of prior work plus an M-convex embedding. This is plausible, but a more self-contained construction would improve confidence and reproducibility.

The contribution is specialized to M-convex action sets. This is a rich class, but the paper does not characterize how restrictive the assumption is in common inverse-optimization applications beyond a few examples.

Reproducibility is adequate for a theoretical paper in terms of definitions and algorithms, but there are no experiments or code, and the practical implementation details for membership-oracle operations, optimization over X_t, and approximate centroids are left high level.

Some limitations are discussed, including the remaining log d gap and stronger corruption models, but the paper could more explicitly discuss when the computational overhead of centroid estimation may dominate the usefulness of the regret improvement.

strengths: The paper identifies a clean structural route to finite regret in online inverse linear optimization by exploiting M-convexity. The use of local exchange optimality to translate observed actions into pairwise order constraints is simple and compelling.

The main O(d log d) regret argument is elegant: choosing the estimate as a center of gravity of the order polytope and applying a volume-shrinkage argument gives a substantial improvement over the warm-up O(d^2) bound and over prior finite bounds exponential in d, within the M-convex setting.

The corruption-robust extension is a useful addition. Detecting inconsistent feedback through cycles in the induced directed graph is natural, does not require prior knowledge of C, and gives an interpretable O((C+1)d log d) bound.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with clear preliminaries, a warm-up algorithm, the refined algorithm, corruption handling, a lower bound, and appendices discussing approximate center-of-gravity computation and computational costs.

The limitations and future directions are treated reasonably honestly, including the remaining log d gap, the stronger corruption models not handled, and the distinction between regret-based evaluation and full parameter estimation.
weaknesses: The contribution is theoretically neat but specialized: the main improvement relies heavily on M-convex action sets and pairwise exchange structure, so the practical scope beyond matroid-like/combinatorial settings is limited.

The computational practicality of the O(d log d) algorithm is weak. Exact center-of-gravity computation is #P-hard, and the proposed randomized approximation has very large polynomial cost, roughly \u007eO(d^6 log d log T) per round plus oracle costs. This makes the headline bound more of an information-theoretic/structural result than a readily usable algorithm.

The corruption section uses a somewhat nonstandard regret definition based on the possibly corrupted observed action xt. Although the paper discusses its relation to regret against the true optimal action, the theorem statement itself can obscure the cost of corrupted rounds, especially since per-round terms need not behave like standard nonnegative regret when xt is suboptimal.

The reproducibility package appears incomplete: Appendix C says 'The code is available at .' with no actual link or artifact. For a paper with an experimental appendix and approximate randomized implementation details, this is a concrete reproducibility weakness.

The empirical evidence is very limited and only illustrative: one small synthetic uniform-matroid experiment with five trials. This is acceptable for a primarily theoretical paper, but it does little to demonstrate practical relevance or robustness of the proposed algorithms.

Several assumptions reduce generality, especially bounded per-round regret and distinct components of w* for corruption detection. The paper explains tied components in the uncorrupted case, but the corrupted case remains dependent on distinctness.

The presentation of implementation details could be sharper. The approximate center-of-gravity algorithm requires failure probabilities depending on T, introduces randomized expected-regret guarantees, and has substantial hidden polylogarithmic factors; these distinctions are not fully reflected in the main theorem statements.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete structural setting, M-convex action sets, in which online inverse linear optimization admits finite regret independent of T. The O(d log d) upper bound is conceptually clean and improves over the earlier exponential finite bound under this restriction.

The main uncorrupted analysis is fairly elegant: Proposition 2.4 reduces optimality to local exchange inequalities, and the center-of-gravity/volume argument gives a plausible route from O(d^2) pairwise learning to O(d log d).

The corruption-robust extension is a nice idea. Monitoring cycles in the directed graph of inferred order constraints is simple, adaptive to unknown C, and reasonably well motivated by the distinct-components assumption.
The paper includes useful appendices on approximate center-of-gravity implementation, computational costs, lower-bound adaptation, and handling tied components in the uncorrupted case.
weaknesses: The contribution is narrower than the framing suggests. The finite polynomial regret result is only for M-convex action sets, while the general open question remains unresolved; the paper sometimes presents this partial resolution in overly strong terms.

The algorithm with the advertised O(d log d) regret relies on center-of-gravity computation over an order polytope. The exact step is #P-hard, and the approximate implementation has very high per-round complexity, roughly \tilde O(d^6 log d log T). This makes the main algorithm mostly theoretical and weakens practical significance.

The assumptions are restrictive and not fully stress-tested. The distinct-components condition is essential for the corruption detector, and the paper only removes it in the uncorrupted case. The per-round regret boundedness assumption is also treated as a simplification, but the dependence on action-set diameter/objective scaling is hidden in O(1).

The corruption model is limited to counting corrupted rounds, and the paper explicitly does not handle cumulative suboptimality corruption as in some prior work. This makes the robustness result less comparable to stronger or more flexible existing robustness formulations.

The empirical section is very weak: a small synthetic experiment with d=20, T=5000, five trials, and uniform matroids only. It does not meaningfully validate the method, explore scaling, test corruption, or support claims of practical usefulness.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Appendix C says the code is available at a blank location, so the experiments are not reproducible from the manuscript. Key implementation details for the randomized center-of-gravity approximation are only sketched.
The lower bound is largely an adaptation of prior work and only matches the upper bound up to a log d factor. This is useful context, but it is not a major independent technical contribution.

Limitations are mentioned, but the paper could be more candid in the main text about computational impracticality, the narrowness of M-convexity relative to general inverse linear optimization, and the unresolved tied-coordinate issue under corruption.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear open problem in online inverse linear optimization: whether finite regret polynomial in dimension is possible. The O(d log d) bound under M-convex action sets is meaningful, clean, and nearly matches the adapted Omega(d) lower bound.

The technical idea is elegant and well motivated. The paper uses the local optimality characterization of M-convex sets to convert observed actions into pairwise ordering constraints, then combines this with a center-of-gravity/volume argument to reduce the mistake bound from O(d^2) to O(d log d).

The corruption-robust extension is a valuable addition. Detecting inconsistent feedback through cycles in the induced directed graph is simple and well aligned with the M-convex structure, and the O((C+1)d log d) guarantee without knowing C is a useful robustness result.

The presentation is generally clear. The paper builds from a warm-up O(d^2) algorithm to the sharper result, gives examples such as matroids and integer-lattice extensions, and explains the role of the assumptions and ties in an appendix.

The work includes computational considerations for approximate center-of-gravity computation and oracle-based implementation, which helps make the theoretical algorithm more reproducible than a purely existential result.
weaknesses: The main result applies only to M-convex feasible sets, so it only partially resolves the broader open question. The paper motivates this class reasonably well, but the practical reach depends on whether real online inverse problems expose such structure and efficient membership/linear-optimization oracles.

The O(d log d) algorithm relies on center-of-gravity computation. Although the appendix gives a randomized approximate implementation, the resulting per-round complexity is high, roughly \tilde O(d^6 log d log T) plus oracle costs, which limits practical usefulness of the strongest bound.

The experimental evidence is very limited: a small synthetic uniform-matroid experiment with d=20, T=5000, and five trials. It is useful as an illustration but not strong evidence of practical superiority, especially given the expensive center-of-gravity machinery.

The reproducibility of the experiment is incomplete in the manuscript: Appendix C says the code is available at a blank placeholder. This should be fixed, and more details on random seeds, instance generation, and implementation choices would be helpful.

The corruption model counts corrupted rounds rather than cumulative suboptimality, and the distinct-components assumption is still needed for the corruption-detection argument. The paper discusses these limitations honestly, but they reduce the generality of the robust result.

Some assumptions are swept into big-O constants, especially bounded per-round regret and oracle access to M-convex sets. These are standard simplifications, but the dependence on feasible-set diameter, encoding size, and oracle complexity should be more explicit in the main theorem statements.
